title: Examining the Seasonal‐Transition Effect on Dissolved Carbon Sources and Exports in a Subtropical Headwater Catchment
content:
Abstract

Unraveling the linkages between stream water sources and dissolved carbon (DC) dynamics is essential for refining the global carbon budget, yet these connections remain poorly constrained. Here, we conducted an 18-month continuous monitoring campaign of stream water, throughfall, soil water, and groundwater from a seasonally distinct headwater catchment in southern China. By analyzing DC concentrations, stable carbon isotopes, water isotopes, and major ions across all water types, we revealed how hydrological seasonality influenced DC dynamics. Results showed a pronounced seasonal shift in stream water sources: groundwater (52.8%) dominated during the dry season, whereas throughfall (49.0%) became the primary contributor in the wet season, followed by 20 cm soil water (24.6%) and groundwater (20.7%). This shift in water sources enhanced shallow and deep soil respiration. Consequently, the contribution of soil organic matter to stream dissolved organic carbon decreased from 91.1% in the dry season to 83.3% in the wet season, while the biogenic contribution to dissolved inorganic carbon increased from 54.5% to 78.7%. Driven by elevated inputs from throughfall, 20 cm soil water and groundwater, DC exports increased significantly in the wet season. The wet season accounted for 68% of annual land-river DC export (12.94 g C m−2 yr−1), 63% of downstream DC export (3.03 g C m−2 yr−1), and 70% of stream CO2 emission (1,505.50 g C m−2 yr−1). Overall, these findings demonstrate that seasonal variations in precipitation and streamflow alter stream water sources and in turn affect stream DC sources and exports. This study underscores the importance of hydrological seasonality in controlling the subtropical carbon cycle, particularly under projected increases in precipitation frequency.
